topics.title: Matter and its properties
topics.unit: Unit 1 – Chemistry: The Study of Matter
topics.concept: Chemistry studies matter and its changes. Matter exists as solid, liquid or gas; properties are physical or chemical, extensive or intensive; pure substances have fixed composition while mixtures are separated by physical methods.

subtopics.title: Chemistry and its branches
subtopics.concept: Main branches: organic, inorganic, physical, analytical, biochemistry, industrial and nuclear chemistry.

textbook_refs.unit: Unit 1 – Chemistry: The Study of Matter

subtopics.title: States of matter and changes of state
subtopics.concept: Melting, freezing, evaporation, condensation; sublimation is the direct change of a solid into a gas (iodine, dry ice, naphthalene).

textbook_refs.unit: Unit 1 – Chemistry: The Study of Matter

subtopics.title: Physical/chemical changes; pure substances and properties
subtopics.concept: Chemical changes form new substances (frying an egg, burning, rusting); physical changes do not (dissolving, melting, magnetic separation, filtration). Elements and compounds (water, O₂, CO₂) have fixed composition; mixtures (air, milk, sea water, steel) do not. Intensive properties (boiling point, % alcohol) do not depend on amount; extensive ones (mass, volume) do.

subtopics.title: Separating mixtures
subtopics.concept: Separation techniques are physical processes based on differences in the physical properties of the components: filtration, evaporation/crystallisation, distillation, fractional distillation, decantation, sublimation, magnetic separation, chromatography, hand picking.

topics.title: Atomic structure, symbols and formulas
topics.concept: Atoms contain a dense nucleus of protons and neutrons surrounded by electrons in shells. Symbols, formulas and names (Stock system, binary acids) follow fixed rules.

subtopics.title: Protons, neutrons, electrons and the nucleus
subtopics.concept: Atomic number = number of protons; protons + neutrons = nucleons, found in the dense nucleus; electrons move in shells (orbits). The neutron is (slightly) the heaviest particle; the proton is positive.

subtopics.title: Electron configuration and isoelectronic species
subtopics.concept: Shells fill 2, 8, 8, 2 for the first 20 elements (Ca = 2, 8, 8, 2). Isoelectronic species have the same number of electrons (O²⁻, F⁻, Na⁺, Mg²⁺, Al³⁺ all have 10).

subtopics.title: Symbols, formulas and names
subtopics.concept: C = carbon. NH₄⁺ is the common positive polyatomic ion. Stock names give the metal's charge: Fe₂O₃ = iron(III) oxide. Binary acids: H₂S(aq) = hydrosulphuric acid. M₂O₃ means M³⁺, so its chloride is MCl₃.

topics.title: The periodic table
topics.concept: Mendeleev arranged elements by atomic mass; the modern table is arranged by atomic number. Metallic and non-metallic character, radius, ionisation energy and electronegativity change periodically.

subtopics.title: Mendeleev's table and groups
subtopics.concept: Mendeleev left gaps and predicted undiscovered elements, but could not fix the position of hydrogen, had no place for isotopes and had irregular pairs. Elements with the same number of valence electrons are in the same group.

textbook_refs.section: 1.1 Mendeleev's periodic table – merits and limitations
1.2 The modern periodic table – groups and periods

subtopics.title: Periodic trends
subtopics.concept: Across a period ionisation energy, electronegativity and non-metallic character increase, atomic size and metallic character decrease. For isoelectronic ions the fewer the protons, the larger the ion (N³⁻ > O²⁻ > F⁻ > Na⁺ > Mg²⁺). Halogens (ns²np⁵) have an incomplete p subshell.

textbook_refs.section: 1.2 The modern periodic table – halogens (group VIIA)

subtopics.title: Properties of metals and non-metals
subtopics.concept: Metals are lustrous (shiny), malleable, ductile, conductors and lose electrons; sodium is soft, very reactive and not brittle. Non-metals are brittle, non-lustrous, gain electrons and form anions.

topics.title: Chemical bonding and intermolecular forces
topics.unit: Unit 2 – Chemical Bonding and Forces of Attraction
topics.concept: Ionic, covalent (non-polar or polar) and metallic bonds; bond energy increases from single to triple bonds; hydrogen bonds form when H is attached to F, O or N.

subtopics.title: Covalent, polar covalent and ionic bonds; bond energy
subtopics.concept: Equal sharing (O₂, Cl₂) = non-polar; unequal sharing between different non-metals (HCl) = polar covalent; metal + non-metal (LiF, MgO) = ionic. Bond energy: C≡C > C=C > C–H > C–O > C–C.

textbook_refs.unit: Unit 2 – Chemical Bonding and Forces of Attraction

subtopics.title: Hydrogen bonding
subtopics.concept: Hydrogen bonds form between molecules with H bonded to a small, very electronegative atom (F, O, N): HF, H₂O, H₂O₂, NH₃. NaH is an ionic hydride (H⁻) and forms no hydrogen bonds.

textbook_refs.unit: Unit 2 – Chemical Bonding and Forces of Attraction

topics.title: Solutions
topics.concept: Solutions are homogeneous mixtures; they are classified by state and by degree of saturation. Concentration can be given as mass percent, molarity or normality; solubility depends on temperature; colligative properties depend on the number of solute particles.

subtopics.title: Types of solutions; saturated, unsaturated and supersaturated
subtopics.concept: A saturated solution cannot dissolve more solute at a given temperature. Liquid solution: sea water; gaseous: air; solid: brass, bronze, steel.

subtopics.title: Mass percent, molarity and normality
subtopics.concept: Mass % = mass solute ÷ (mass solute + mass solvent) × 100. Molarity = mol solute ÷ L solution. Normality N = equivalents ÷ L; in titrations N₁V₁ = N₂V₂.

subtopics.title: Solubility and the effect of temperature
subtopics.concept: Temperature changes solubility (usually increases it for solids, decreases it for gases). Nitrates, ammonium and alkali-metal salts are soluble; most carbonates (CaCO₃) are insoluble.

subtopics.title: Colligative properties
subtopics.concept: Vapour-pressure lowering, boiling-point elevation, freezing-point depression and osmotic pressure depend only on the number of solute particles – colour is not colligative.

topics.title: Acids, bases and salts
topics.concept: Acids taste sour and donate protons; bases taste bitter, feel slippery and accept protons. pH 7 is neutral. Titration uses an indicator to find the end point, which approximates the equivalence point.

subtopics.title: Properties and definitions of acids and bases
subtopics.concept: Bases: bitter, slippery, turn litmus blue, pH > 7, neutralise acids. Brønsted–Lowry: acid = proton donor, base = proton acceptor (NH₃ + H⁺ → NH₄⁺). Oxides of active metals give basic solutions. Concentrated sulphuric acid is highly corrosive; acetic acid is a weak acid (vinegar contains CH₃COOH, H₃O⁺ and CH₃COO⁻).

textbook_refs.section: 4.1 Brønsted–Lowry definition of acids and bases

subtopics.title: Titration: normality, end point and equivalence point
subtopics.concept: Equivalence point: equivalents of acid = equivalents of base. End point: where the indicator changes colour. N₁V₁ = N₂V₂.

textbook_refs.section: 4.4 Titration – end point and equivalence point

topics.title: Energy and chemical reactions
topics.concept: Chemical energy is potential energy stored in bonds. Heat flows from hot to cold. Exothermic reactions release heat (ΔH < 0); endothermic reactions absorb heat (ΔH > 0).

subtopics.title: Forms of energy and heat flow
subtopics.concept: Chemical energy is potential energy. Heat flows from the hotter object to the colder one until their temperatures are equal.

subtopics.title: Exothermic and endothermic reactions and energy diagrams
subtopics.concept: Exothermic: heat given off, products have less energy, ΔH negative, surroundings get warmer. Endothermic: heat absorbed, ΔH positive, surroundings get cooler. On an energy diagram ΔH is the difference between the reactant and product levels; activation energy is from the reactants to the peak.

textbook_refs.section: 5.2 Energy diagrams of exothermic and endothermic reactions

topics.title: Chemical equilibrium
topics.unit: Unit 1 – Rate of a Chemical Reaction and Factors Affecting it
topics.concept: Reversible reactions reach dynamic equilibrium when the forward and backward rates are equal. The equilibrium constant is products over reactants, each raised to its coefficient.

subtopics.title: Dynamic equilibrium and the equilibrium constant
subtopics.concept: At equilibrium, forward rate = backward rate and concentrations stay constant (not necessarily equal). For aA + bB ⇌ cC, Kc = [C]ᶜ/([A]ᵃ[B]ᵇ).

textbook_refs.unit: Unit 1 – Rate of a Chemical Reaction and Factors Affecting it

topics.title: Oxidation–reduction and electrolysis
topics.concept: Oxidation = addition of oxygen, removal of hydrogen, loss of electrons, increase in oxidation number. The oxidising agent gains electrons and is reduced. In electrolysis, oxidation occurs at the anode, reduction at the cathode.

subtopics.title: Oxidation, oxidation numbers and redox reactions
subtopics.concept: Oxidising agent: gains electrons, causes oxidation, is itself reduced. C in CaCO₃ is +4. Double-displacement (precipitation) reactions such as AgNO₃ + NaCl are not redox.

subtopics.title: Electrolysis
subtopics.concept: Anode = positive electrode (oxidation), cathode = negative electrode (reduction). Anions move to the anode, cations to the cathode.

topics.title: Nonmetals and their compounds
topics.unit: Unit 3 – Chemistry of Some Nonmetals and Their Compounds
topics.concept: Carbon (allotropes, amorphous forms, CO, CO₂), nitrogen (nitrogen cycle, Haber process) and sulphur compounds (sulphuric acid).

subtopics.title: Amorphous carbon, carbon monoxide and carbon dioxide
subtopics.concept: Amorphous carbon: coke, wood charcoal, animal charcoal, carbon black. CO is colourless, odourless, neutral and a good reducing agent. CO₂ uses: photosynthesis, refrigeration (dry ice), beverages, fire extinguishers.

subtopics.title: Nitrogen cycle and the Haber process
subtopics.concept: Organisms cannot use atmospheric N₂ directly; soil bacteria convert it into ammonium and nitrate compounds that plants use. Haber process: N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ with an iron catalyst.

subtopics.title: Sulphuric acid
subtopics.concept: A strong, dense, oily, highly corrosive acid; concentrated H₂SO₄ is a dehydrating and oxidising agent.

textbook_refs.unit: Unit 3 – Chemistry of Some Nonmetals and Their Compounds

topics.title: Metals and metallurgy
topics.unit: Unit 4 – Chemistry of Some Metals and Their Compounds
topics.concept: Reactivity of metals with water and acids follows the activity series. Metallurgy: ores (bauxite, haematite, chalcopyrite, galena, calamine), concentration, roasting/calcination, reduction (carbon for Fe, Zn, Pb; electrolysis for Na, Al) and refining.

subtopics.title: Activity series, reactions with water and uses
subtopics.concept: K, Na, Ca react with cold water; Mg with hot water; Al, Zn, Fe with steam; Pb, Cu, Ag, Au, Pt do not react with water at all. Aluminium is light, strong, corrosion-resistant and a good conductor: foil, cans, utensils, aircraft, power cables, window frames.

textbook_refs.unit: Unit 4 – Chemistry of Some Metals and Their Compounds
Unit 4 – Chemistry of Some Metals and Their Compounds

subtopics.title: Ores, calcination and reduction
subtopics.concept: Bauxite → Al, haematite → Fe, chalcopyrite → Cu, galena → Pb, calamine → Zn. Roasting: sulphide ore in excess air; calcination: carbonate ore heated strongly in limited air. Carbon (coke) reduces oxides of Fe, Zn, Pb; very reactive metals (Na, Mg, Al) need electrolysis.

topics.title: Behaviour of gases
topics.concept: Gases expand, are compressible, have low density and diffuse rapidly. Gas laws: Boyle (P ∝ 1/V), Charles (V ∝ T), Avogadro (V ∝ n), combined gas law P₁V₁/T₁ = P₂V₂/T₂.

subtopics.title: Gas laws and the combined gas law
subtopics.concept: Boyle: halving the volume doubles the pressure (T constant). Avogadro: V ∝ n at constant T and P. Combined: P₁V₁/T₁ = P₂V₂/T₂ with T in kelvin.

subtopics.title: Properties of gases and kinetic molecular theory
subtopics.concept: Gases expand indefinitely, are easily compressed, have low density and diffuse rapidly. The average kinetic energy of the molecules depends only on the absolute temperature.

topics.title: Shapes of molecules and crystals
topics.unit: Unit 1 – Shapes of Simple Molecules and Crystals
topics.concept: VSEPR predicts electron-pair and molecular geometries; solids are crystalline or amorphous (glass).

subtopics.title: VSEPR assumptions and shapes
subtopics.concept: Repulsions: lone pair–lone pair > lone pair–bond pair > bond pair–bond pair; repulsion decreases as the inter-pair angle increases. With no lone pairs the electron-pair and molecular geometries are the same (BF₃ trigonal planar).

textbook_refs.unit: Unit 1 – Shapes of Simple Molecules and Crystals
Unit 1 – Shapes of Simple Molecules and Crystals
textbook_refs.section: 1.1 VSEPR – shapes with and without non-bonding pairs

subtopics.title: Crystalline and amorphous solids
subtopics.concept: Crystalline solids (NaCl, sugar, sulphur, diamond) have regular arrangements and sharp melting points; glass is amorphous.

textbook_refs.unit: Unit 1 – Shapes of Simple Molecules and Crystals

topics.title: Organic chemistry
topics.concept: Organic chemistry began with Wöhler's urea synthesis. Hydrocarbons: alkanes, alkenes, alkynes, cycloalkanes; isomerism; petroleum refining (cracking); functional groups.

subtopics.title: Hydrocarbons, isomerism, naming and cracking
subtopics.concept: Alkynes CₙH₂ₙ₋₂ (C₄H₆); cycloalkanes CₙH₂ₙ (n ≥ 3). Isomers have the same molecular formula but different structures; geometric (cis–trans) isomerism needs two different groups on each C of the double bond (1-butene has none). Cracking breaks large alkanes into smaller alkanes and alkenes.

subtopics.title: Functional groups and the origin of organic chemistry
subtopics.concept: Names ending in -al are aldehydes (pentanal), -one ketones, -ol alcohols, -oic acid carboxylic acids. Wöhler (1828) made urea by heating ammonium cyanate.

topics.title: Nuclear chemistry
topics.concept: Nuclear reactions involve the nucleus (protons and neutrons), large energy changes and loss of mass. Radioactive decay emits α, β or γ radiation; fission splits a heavy nucleus.

subtopics.title: Nuclear reactions and radioactive decay
subtopics.concept: Nuclear reactions involve protons and neutrons, very large energy changes and loss of mass, and are irreversible. α, β and γ decay are radioactive; ionisation of sodium is a chemical change.

textbook_refs.section: Introduction – Table 3.1 Comparison of chemical and nuclear reactions

subtopics.title: Nuclear fission and fusion
subtopics.concept: Fission: a heavy nucleus splits into lighter, more stable nuclei with release of energy; fusion joins light nuclei.
